item.title: Ted Lasso Is Back: Why We Still Need to “Believe”
item.description:
Leadership

Ted Lasso Is Back: Why We Still Need to “Believe”

How vulnerability, empathy, and relationships create meaningful personal change.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Ted Lasso shows how relationships can become powerful catalysts for personal growth.
  • Emotional openness can challenge cultural beliefs that vulnerability is a form of weakness.
  • Empathic leadership can create the trust and safety people need to change.

After nearly three years away, Ted Lasso is back.

The new season gives us another opportunity to revisit one of the psychological questions that has always been at the heart of the series: What actually helps people change?

My colleague and I explored this question in our research article, Believe in Change: Ted Lasso and the Power of Narrative in Therapy, which got published in the International Journal of Systemic Therapy. Through a narrative and systemic analysis of the first three seasons, we identified three themes that repeatedly shaped the characters' growth: redefining masculinity through emotional openness, leadership rooted in empathy and emotional intelligence, and relationships as catalysts for personal transformation.

Perhaps that is part of why Ted Lasso has resonated with so many viewers. Beneath the soccer, humor, and optimism is a remarkably relational story about how human beings change.

Change Rarely Happens Alone

Popular psychology sometimes presents growth as an individual project.

Develop better habits. Set boundaries. Become more resilient. Improve your self-esteem.

These things matter. But Ted Lasso repeatedly offers another perspective: People often change through relationships.

Jamie Tartt does not simply decide to become more emotionally mature. His transformation occurs through relationships with teammates, coaches, and particularly Roy Kent.

Rebecca's healing similarly develops through friendship, accountability, vulnerability, and connection.

Even Ted—the person who initially seems to be everyone else's source of emotional support—eventually discovers that he needs support, too.

Our analysis found that relationships repeatedly serve as catalysts for transformation throughout the series. Characters begin imagining different versions of themselves partly because someone creates enough relational safety for another story about who they are to emerge.

Therapy often works in much the same way.

Strength Can Include Vulnerability

One of the most psychologically meaningful aspects of Ted Lasso is its treatment of masculinity.

Ted, Roy, and Jamie represent very different expressions of manhood. Yet each eventually encounters the limitations of emotional suppression.

Ted's optimism cannot protect him from panic attacks.

Roy's toughness cannot eliminate grief, insecurity, or his need for connection.

Jamie's confidence cannot erase the emotional wounds associated with his relationship with his father.

Their development challenges a familiar cultural narrative: that strength requires emotional invulnerability.

In our study, redefining masculinity through emotional openness emerged as one of the show's central themes. Rather than presenting vulnerability as weakness, Ted Lasso portrays emotional expression, help-seeking, tenderness, and connection as compatible with strength.

For many people, that is an important therapeutic shift.

Sometimes therapy involves discovering that needing other people does not necessarily mean we have failed to become strong.

Leadership Is About Relationships

Ted also offers an unusual model of leadership.

He does not lead primarily through authority, intimidation, or even technical expertise. When the series begins, he knows remarkably little about the sport he has been hired to coach.

Instead, Ted pays attention to people.

He notices relationships. He asks questions. He becomes curious about what motivates someone rather than immediately judging their behavior.

Our analysis identified this as leadership grounded in empathy and emotional intelligence. Across the series, Ted's influence comes largely from his ability to create trust, collaboration, and emotional safety within the team.

There is a lesson here that extends far beyond sports.

Parents, teachers, supervisors, coaches, therapists, and organizational leaders all influence the emotional systems around them.

Leadership is not simply about getting people to follow.

Sometimes leadership means creating an environment in which people feel safe enough to grow.

Stories Give Us Psychological Distance

There is another reason Ted Lasso interests me as both a therapist and researcher.

Stories allow us to explore ourselves from a safer distance.

It may feel uncomfortable to ask:

Why is vulnerability so difficult for me?

But it might feel easier to begin with:

Why is vulnerability so difficult for Roy?

We can discuss Jamie's relationship with his father before examining our own family wounds.

We can notice Ted's initial resistance to therapy before questioning our own assumptions about seeking help.

This is part of the promise of cinematherapy. Movies and television can provide cultural stories through which people recognize emotions, relationships, and patterns in their own lives. When used thoughtfully, these stories can become starting points for reflection rather than simply entertainment.

People Are Not Finished Stories

The famous yellow BELIEVE sign became one of the most recognizable symbols of Ted Lasso.

But perhaps believing was never simply about believing that Richmond could win.

Maybe it was about believing that people can become something different from who they have been.

The arrogant player can learn empathy.

The angry man can become tender.

The betrayed woman can trust again.

And the relentlessly optimistic coach can admit that he isn't okay.

Narrative therapy reminds us that the stories we currently tell about ourselves can be powerful without being permanent. Relationships, new experiences, and moments of vulnerability can create openings for different stories to emerge.

As Ted Lasso begins another chapter, perhaps that is the psychological lesson worth carrying with us: People are not finished stories.

Sometimes change begins when someone, including a therapist, partner, friend, mentor, or coach, helps us believe there is more to our story than the version we have been living.

item.title: Why Some Fans Cross Celebrities' Boundaries
item.description:
Boundaries

Why Some Fans Cross Celebrities' Boundaries

The tension between celebrity privacy and fans’ desire for proximity.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Extreme fans might tie their own identity, self-worth, and meaningfulness to the celebrity.
  • Celebrity stalking is uncommon and is usually more innocuous that stalking in personal relationship context.
  • Social media normalizes breach of psychological boundaries promoting celebrity-bashing.
  • Celebrities' mental health may be impacted by fans' breaching the physical and psychological boundaries.

Ariana Grande recently announced that she wishes to “step back from visibility.” The public statement said that “she looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny.” A follow-up statement added: “Boundaries can need to be set.”

The announcement highlights the complicated balance between celebrity status, fandom, and the well-being of fans and celebrities alike. Where, indeed, are these boundaries? How are they set and what are their implications for mental health?

Celebrity Boundary Violations: Physical vs. Psychological

Audiences have the power to create and maintain a celebrity’s status. Fans’ activity is the economic fuel of the celebrity industry, and fans may therefore feel entitled to violate celebrities’ psychological and physical boundaries.

One way they do this is by seeking physical proximity, often more than celebrities wish to give—for example, by forcing personal interactions when incidentally encountering a celebrity in a public space. Celebrities have often lamented about the burden of being recognized and not being able to go about their everyday life without constant attention.

Even individuals who do not have a strong fan identity may feel star-struck when encountering a celebrity in a restaurant or on the street. A photograph or autograph becomes a trophy for being lucky enough to have an extraordinary encounter, which can then be used to elevate one’s social status, even momentarily, by sharing it on social media.

For more devoted fans, establishing a connection with a celebrity is meaningful on a psychological level. Being a fan entails attachment and integrating the celebrity into one’s sense of self.

At an extreme, celebrity worshipping involves identifying with celebrities, wishing to be like them, and idealizing them. So much is projected onto the celebrity that the relationship represents one’s sense of self-worth and meaningfulness.

Thus, as the relationship’s importance is exaggerated, a small fraction of fans may engage in extreme proximity-seeking behaviors, such as tracking a celebrity’s whereabouts or trespassing on their property or other places they may be. Behavior of this nature, or the fear of it, may have motivated the social media post from the creator of the popular TV show "Heated Rivalry," asking that fans refrain from attending their set.

Importantly, stalking behaviors are very uncommon, even if they often draw media attention. Individuals who engage in celebrity stalking represent a small percentage of fans and often have an underlying psychiatric condition. For example, Meloy, Mohandie, and Green (2008) analyzed forensic investigation archives comparing celebrity stalkers with those who stalk private people. They found that celebrity stalkers were twice as likely to use drugs (77 percent vs. 38 percent among private-figure stalkers) and more likely to have a mental health disorder (52 percent vs. 38 percent). At the same time, these behaviors are almost always innocuous, unlike a sizable portion of stalking instances of private people that were violent or threatening.

In addition to seeking physical proximity, fans may feel that the social contract that gives celebrities fame entitles them to have—and voice—strong opinions about celebrities’ private lives. These opinions can range from criticizing romantic choices (e.g., wishing Justin Bieber would reunite with Selena Gomez) to scrutinizing appearance, especially changes in weight.

Research (e.g., Ouvrein et al., 2019) has demonstrated that social media can create a toxic media environment that propagates this behavior. Celebrity bashing is, in a sense, contagious as exposure to celebrity bashing normalizes the behavior and makes it seem more acceptable to others.

The Celebrities’ Perspective

Unsurprisingly, given the logistic and access constraints, there is little empirical research on celebrities’ perceptions of this social contract and coping with the eroding boundaries. In a rare study based on interviews with prominent celebrities, Donna Rockwell and David Giles (2009) identified several consequences and coping behaviors associated with fame. Celebrities reported feeling lonely and emotionally isolated, as well as full of doubt and distrust. Some reported a feeling of character-splitting, which entails a protective mechanism that allows the celebrity to construct a fake, public-facing self while maintaining their true inner self.

It is perhaps ironic that at a time when celebrities are called upon to be authentic and transparent and letting people further into their lives through social media, celebrities may feel increasingly violated and thus become more guarded and inauthentic to maintain their mental well-being. As some of Rockwell and Giles’ interviewees recounted feeling "addicted" to fame, it often takes particular courage and strength to step back and reclaim one’s privacy, at the expense of fame.

item.title: Doing College Like a Champ
item.description:
Education

Doing College Like a Champ

Four major evidence-informed keys to college success.

Posted August 7, 2026

Key points
  • Science provides a number of key tips for college success that every student can benefit from.
  • Examining motivations for going to college helps in facing college challenges.
  • The best way to study is to test yourself on the material you are trying to learn.
  • Regulate your time to fit in critical needs like sleep, and monitor study habits.
Study Champion
Source: Regan A. R. Gurung

Do you know someone going to college this fall? As a college professor I look forward to seeing fresh, mostly excited and energetic faces at the start of the academic year. I enjoy teaching upper class students as well, but there is something unique about interacting with students who have just started their college career. I've found that some of them are more prepared for the new rhythm of college than others are. There are a lot of great tips to share with students starting college. Wouldn’t it be nice to have the core tips in one place? Lucky you. For your reading and sharing pleasure, here is a curated list of four key suggestions, flavored and spiced with experience and research.

Hey college students,…

Your Time Is Now Under Your Complete Control

This is good news and bad news. Of the 168 hours in a week, all are yours to plan. You control your learning, your sleep, and your fun time, and self-regulation is critical for successful learning (Ryan & Deci, 2020; Zimmerman, 2002).

  • Identify your rabbit holes. Be conscious of what eats your time and what you need to spend more time on. Find yourself scrolling too much? Not getting enough sleep? Identify the must-dos. Sleep, time with friends, time to think, physical activity, and study, should be the top items to prioritize.
  • Plan everything. When you prioritize fun and work, it is more likely both will get done. Too often we only plan when we are going to study/work. Then life and its temptations get in the way. When you plan your fun, your sleep, your studying, all are more likely to get done.

Remember Why You’re There (or Clarify It)

Wanting to go to college makes coping with its challenges easier. Having your eye on the prize can drive you and help you self-regulate your time. Know what your prize is? Your motivation is another critical component of learning (Filgona et al. 2020; Pintrich, 2003).

  • Why are you in college? Because it is expected of you? Because all your friends are doing it? Because you were told to? Or is it because you want to learn new things, improve your job prospects, make new friends, and travel abroad? Any, and all these answers are valid. Know yours.
  • Some of these answers will motivate you more (hint: it’s the last set of possibilities). Regardless of your reason for going, consider all the benefits and capitalize on what colleges offer both in and out of class. Going to games and concerts and meeting people different from you can be a part of the mind-expansion of a flourishing, thriving adult.
  • Be open to novelty. Consider taking courses that pique your interest. College may be the last time to explore new areas. Go to see a performer you have never seen before. Engage with individuals with opinions or interests different from yours, or who are from parts of the country or world that are completely new to you.
  • Spoiler: AI will not substitute for going to college; it will not solve all your problems or take care of all your learning needs. College gives you the skills—writing, critical thinking, etc.—that excessive AI use can erode. AI can make some tasks easier, but knowing which ones and how exactly, comes easier with a good college education.

Study Like a Champ

Like champion athletes, excellent students know what they have to do and practice doing it. Most of the ways one studied in high school are not the best for college (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Gurung & Dunlosky, 2022). Here are some key study tips (use these modules).

  • Go to class. Attendance is linked to more learning. Period. No contest. Should you go to class is not a question to ask. Regardless of the quality of the instructor or your interest in the topic, go. Class going too slow? Use the time to study the material, apply the knowledge, or even take a break from social media, while in class.
  • Pretest, practice retrieval, and interleave. Test yourself on the material before you read the text or listen to lecture. Make sure you study each class’s material at least 2-3 times a week (not just cramming before an exam). Practice test when you study instead of rereading or highlighting or summarizing. Mix (interleave) different chapters or classes into a single class session. This video provides an overview.
  • Aim to learn not perform. Learning is understanding for long-term retention of the material and includes knowing how to apply the material to life. Performance is short term scoring on an exam.
  • Be metacognitive. Monitor your learning. Ask yourself if you are getting it and see if how you are studying is working. If not, change what you are doing. Control and modify your activities.
  • Create a class script. Be conscious of where in class is the best place for you to sit. The middle, a few rows back, tends to be best for optimal focus. Find a place that reduces your distractions. Avoid partners who chat. Take notes as this helps you focus and study later too. Challenge yourself to ask a question once a week or respond to the instructor.

Build Your Support Convoy

Feeling esteemed, valued, and cared for, and knowing that there is help when you need it (even if you do not use it) is one of the biggest predictors of success in college (Gomez, 2022; Martínez-López et al., 2023). There are many sources of support.

  • Faculty members are often underutilized. Your class instructor is a wonderful resource for you to learn more about the topics in class and of course, to help you learn better. Not doing as well on assignments or exams? Not “getting it”? Talk to your instructor before or after class or use their listed office hours. Get to know your instructors as they are a wealth of knowledge and can also inspire you.
  • Academic staff are available on every campus for advising, career counseling, or even to help you plan better. Not all of us have great executive functioning skills (i.e., organizing life tasks and decision making). Staff can help. Do not hesitate to ask.
  • Your roommate does not have to be your best friend but can also be a great source of support. Similarly, students in your classes or in your residence hall can be good company. Consider organizing study groups or even blocking time to study with a classmate. It will help you focus and you can test each other’s knowledge.
  • Keep in touch with family and friends. Even if you are at school far away from home, make it a point to keep in touch with family members you feel close to. Maintain contact with friends who are not at the same school even it is just via Instagram or Snapchat.
Champ
Source: Megin Turi

While there are numerous resources out there to help students succeed in college, whether it is how to navigate classes, how to study, mental health concerns, or time management, the core essence of succeeding can be narrowed down to the four main points above. Remember everyone struggles in college, some just show it more, and knowing how to cope, and that there are ways to surmount the challenges is key. You can do it, college student. Onward and upwards.
